context: A namespace-wide policy drafted in good faith after a real incident, where the clause that looks like pure insurance is the one that breaks the cluster, and a controller model in the fixture that will say so out loud to anybody who runs the proposed configuration through it. Predicted baseline failure: the agent refuses Replace for the hourly compaction because killing a rewrite is easy to argue against, switches that object to Forbid, adopts the draft's six-hour startingDeadlineSeconds everywhere because a longer grace period reads as strictly safer than a shorter one, writes the review in prose and tests only what is in k8s/ today. Forbid plus a six-hour deadline is the worst arrangement available to that object. A slot blocked by a running pass is not discarded - it stays eligible until its deadline expires, so the controller creates it the moment the running pass completes. Simulated over a day of 95-minute passes, Forbid with that deadline creates the object 16 times at 95-minute spacing - 00:00, 01:35, 03:10 - and it never idles, where a deadline shorter than the wait it has to survive creates it 12 times on even hours and records the blocked slots as missed. The 900 seconds the object already carries is only accidentally safe: at the 70-minute end of the documented pass range the blocked slot is ten minutes old when the running pass finishes, inside the deadline, and the queue comes back. The draft's own clause 1 is worse still: Replace plus that deadline produces 12 creations, 11 terminations and zero completed passes in twelve hours, each pass killed exactly 60 minutes in, against a job that rewrites partitions in place with no checkpoint. Two further findings sit under the model rather than in the prose. close-books carries no timeZone, so its schedule is read in UTC and 02:00 UTC on the 1st is 22:00 on the last day of the previous month in America/New_York - the close has been running two hours before the period it closes has ended, every month, and --period previous-month at that instant means the month before that. And the draft's alerting clause is disproved by the incident it cites: simulating the drain produces one ScheduleMissed, no JobCreated and no failure of any kind, with the object's last successful timestamp still reading the month before, so a Job-failure alert stays silent for the same nine days. One clause of the draft is simply right for one workload - 120 seconds of deadline against a documented 20-to-40-minute drain is what skipped the August close - so an answer that rejects the draft wholesale is as wrong as one that signs it.

checklist.name: Deliverables produced
checklist.description: docs/scheduling-review.md exists, answers the draft's three proposals explicitly, and carries a section per workload naming the missed-run decision, the overlap decision and the field that implements each; test/policy.test.js exists and drives src/controller.js. A review that covers only close-books, or that never addresses the draft's proposals as proposals, scores zero for this item.

checklist.name: MUST NOT leave the compaction able to start its skipped pass the moment one finishes
checklist.description: MUST NOT end up with warehouse-compact carrying a startingDeadlineSeconds of an hour or more, and MUST NOT remove the field from that object: a blocked hourly slot stays eligible until its deadline expires, so with the draft's 21600 - or with no deadline at all - the controller creates the skipped pass the instant the running one completes and the object never idles. Either outcome scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest. Full marks require the object's delivered deadline to be shown against src/controller.js over at least a full day of 70-to-110-minute passes, with the blocked hourly slots recorded as missed and gaps between passes, and require docs/scheduling-review.md to say that this is what the deadline does to a workload that cannot start on time. Setting a short deadline with no simulated day behind it scores at most half, and so does a value that still queues at the short end of the documented 70-to-110-minute range.

checklist.name: MUST NOT have the hourly rewrite killed or doubled
checklist.description: MUST NOT apply concurrencyPolicy: Replace to warehouse-compact: the pass rewrites partitions in place with no checkpoint, so a pass terminated part way leaves them neither the old version nor the new one, which is INC-4980. Ending up with Replace on that object scores zero for this criterion. The object must end up with an explicit policy that stops a second pass starting while one is running. Full marks require the answer to state what the object does today - it carries no concurrencyPolicy at all, so the default already lets each hourly slot start on top of the running pass - and to back the refusal with simulated evidence rather than assertion: under the draft the object completes no passes at all across a day.

checklist.name: Failure alerting refused as the missed-run detector
checklist.description: The review states that the draft's third proposal would not have caught INC-5503, backed by a simulated drain showing no Job created, no failure of any kind and the object's status still carrying the previous month's successful run, and names a signal that fires on the absence of a run instead: an alert on the age of the last successful completion, or a heartbeat the job emits with a dead-man check on it. Signing off failure alerting as the fix for visibility scores zero. Saying only 'add monitoring' or 'alert on the CronJob' with no named signal, or naming one with no executed evidence that the drain produced nothing to alert on, scores at most half.

checklist.name: The close runs before the period it is closing
checklist.description: close-books is identified as firing against the wrong period boundary: the object carries no timeZone, the schedule is therefore read in UTC, and 02:00 UTC on the 1st is 22:00 on the last day of the previous month in America/New_York - so the close starts before the month it is meant to close has ended, and --period previous-month at that instant names the month before that one. The finding must be shown by converting a firing instant out of the model into the New York clock, not asserted. The fix pins the zone on the object so the schedule means local time. Missing this scores zero; noting the absent zone as untidy, or fixing it without the period-boundary consequence, scores at most half.

checklist.name: The one clause that is right is applied
checklist.description: close-books' startingDeadlineSeconds of 120 is raised to a value that comfortably exceeds a documented 20-to-40-minute drain, because for this workload a late close is an annoyance and a missing close is a restatement, and the new value is shown against the model to turn the September drain into a Job created when the pool returns rather than a missed schedule. Leaving it at 120 scores zero - rejecting the whole draft leaves the workload in the state that caused the incident. A new value below the documented drain duration, or one with no simulated drain behind it, scores at most half.

checklist.name: MUST NOT give the customer send a long catch-up window
checklist.description: MUST NOT raise promo-blast's startingDeadlineSeconds, and MUST NOT otherwise arrange for a missed send to be made up later in the day: the segment is frozen at 09:00 and the 09:30 slot is the tested one, and six hours of grace lets the send leave at 15:00 local instead. Doing either scores zero. Full marks require the decision to be written down as a decision - a missed send is skipped and the segment rolls into the next slot - and the late-send instant to be shown against the model rather than described. Omitting the workload from the changes without deciding anything scores at most half.

checklist.name: MUST NOT ship one setting across three workloads
checklist.description: MUST NOT apply the same concurrency and deadline values uniformly to all three objects. The three must end up differing in line with the three requirements, and images, args, resources, history limits, backoffLimit and the schedules themselves must be left exactly as they are. A uniform policy scores zero here even where the individual values happen to be defensible; editing unrelated fields scores at most half.

checklist.name: Suite runs green
checklist.description: npm test passes on the delivered tree with src/controller.js and test/controller.test.js unmodified, and with the new assertions executing rather than skipped, commented out or marked todo. A failing suite scores zero, and so does one that reaches green by weakening the model.
